section_summary: This section follows Japan’s 1932 budget crisis: borrowing for operations in Manchuria, military expansion and rural relief raised concern about debt, inflation and the yen. Embassy reports, State Department summaries and Japanese press translations examine the supplementary budgets and competing proposals for loans, taxation and spending cuts. The section also contains material on Manchukuo’s recognition, capital controls, and confidential forwarding of reports on developments in Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Interpellations in the Lower House on recognition of Manchukuo
subfiles.about: Matsuoka urges immediate recognition of Manchukuo and Premier Saitō replies.
subfiles.summary: Saitō says the government intends to recognize the new state as soon as possible.

subfiles.title: House of Peers Budget Committee interpellations on Manchukuo
subfiles.about: Baron Ida questions whether approving the supplementary budget amounts to recognizing Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Saitō says recognition awaits arrangements, including protection of Japanese residents in Manchuria. Most additional spending supports Japanese forces there; the final fragment addresses a hypothetical emergency.

subfiles.title: Lower House Budget Committee interpellations
subfiles.about: Kodama questions Saitō about an Associated Press interview on Manchuria and international agreements.
subfiles.summary: Saitō discusses possible League withdrawal and early recognition of Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: File note on Bank of Japan currency issue
subfiles.about: A cross-reference points to a despatch on expanded Bank of Japan note issuance.
subfiles.summary: Expanded note issuance would finance Army activity and agrarian relief.

subfiles.title: File note on capital-flight legislation
subfiles.about: A cross-reference points to the convertible bank note and capital-flight laws.
subfiles.summary: Notes laws effective July 1, 1932.

subfiles.title: Summary of pending Japanese budget and relief measures
subfiles.about: The summary considers planned borrowing, tax proposals and relief expenditures.
subfiles.summary: Japan faces a large budget deficit, heavy reliance on bonds and possible inflation. Proposed relief loans address farmers, smaller businesses and frozen realty credit, while party opposition may complicate passage.

subfiles.title: Proposed supplementary budget and three-year relief program
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The embassy details proposed supplementary spending, bond financing and a three-year relief program.
subfiles.summary: The proposed budget provides about 175 million yen in national spending, chiefly public works, with further prefectural expenditures and extra-budgetary credit relief. Grew explains the prospective bond issues, departmental allocations and Takahashi’s three-year program, then assesses possible Diet opposition.

subfiles.title: Supplementary budget estimates passed by the 63rd Diet
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The embassy transmits the enacted supplementary budget and special-account estimates.
subfiles.summary: The translated figures detail departmental expenditure, national loans and accounts for Korea, Taiwan and Sakhalin. Grew notes an unexplained gap between revenue and expenditure and uncertainty about how territorial loans are counted.

subfiles.title: Summary of Japan’s indebtedness and currency position
subfiles.about: A departmental précis evaluates relief loans, public debt, yen depreciation and Japan’s external finances.
subfiles.summary: The précis calls relief measures inadequate, describes rising debt and distinguishes yen depreciation from actual currency inflation. It notes temporary gains for producers but warns of poor foreign credit, boycotts and mounting pressure on external payments.

subfiles.title: Japan’s economic and financial condition
subfiles.about: A long embassy report reviews rural debt, relief, national borrowing, currency depreciation and financial pressure abroad.
subfiles.summary: Farmers, merchants and small manufacturers carry heavy debts, while the government plans public works and credit relief financed largely through bonds. The report surveys a decade of national debt and laws enabling expanded Bank of Japan bond purchases and capital controls. It credits the weaker yen and stronger rice and silk prices with temporary domestic relief, but finds foreign obligations, weak credit and trade boycotts serious longer-term pressures.

subfiles.title: Summary of diplomatic corps obligations under the capital-flight law
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes Japan’s requirement that diplomats seek permission for foreign-currency accounts.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo’s despatch encloses the Japanese circular and application requirements.

subfiles.title: Despatch on application of capital-flight law to diplomats
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports that diplomatic personnel are subject to Japan’s foreign-currency account rules.
subfiles.summary: The despatch forwards French and English versions of the circular.

subfiles.title: Japanese Foreign Office circular, French translation
subfiles.about: The circular explains how diplomats should comply with Japan’s capital-flight law.
subfiles.summary: Diplomats must apply through banks to retain foreign-currency accounts.

subfiles.title: Japanese Foreign Office circular, English translation
subfiles.about: The English translation repeats the requirement for diplomats’ foreign-currency accounts.
subfiles.summary: The Finance Ministry promises to review applications sympathetically.

subfiles.title: Article 4 of Finance Ministry Decree No. 13
subfiles.about: The decree lists information required for authorization of foreign-currency accounts or loans.
subfiles.summary: Applications must identify the parties, amounts, terms and purpose.

subfiles.title: Political report on the extraordinary Diet session
subfiles.about: The report describes political opposition to the government’s rural relief program.
subfiles.summary: Seiyūkai and Kokumin Dōmei members challenge the proposed relief total.

subfiles.title: Political report section on government finance
subfiles.about: The excerpt summarizes relief borrowing and projected annual budget totals.
subfiles.summary: Bond-financed relief raises projected borrowing above 700 million yen.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese special budget bill
subfiles.about: A cross-reference identifies a report on Japan’s special budget bill.
subfiles.summary: Points to political report No. 145.

subfiles.title: Political report section on the special budget
subfiles.about: The excerpt notes the unexplained surplus in the special budget as passed.
subfiles.summary: Revenue exceeded spending by roughly 17 million yen.

subfiles.title: Summary of despatch on Japan’s budgetary difficulties
subfiles.about: A State Department summary highlights the projected 1933 budget deficit and military claims.
subfiles.summary: New claims could push spending to about 2.5 billion yen against 1.25 billion yen in revenue. The summary emphasizes rising bond debt, resistance to taxes and the Army’s refusal to cut its demands.

subfiles.title: Japan’s budgetary difficulties
subfiles.about: The embassy analyzes unprecedented ministry claims against the next fiscal year’s budget.
subfiles.summary: Projected spending would leave a deficit exceeding a billion yen. The report traces rapid debt growth after Inoue’s deflation policy, weighs taxation against further bonds and describes the Army’s powerful position in budget negotiations. It also notes signs of public and political unease.

subfiles.title: Telegram on opposition to proposed bond issue
subfiles.about: The embassy reports growing opposition to borrowing nearly a billion yen for the next fiscal year.
subfiles.summary: Newspapers and economists warn that military demands threaten financial stability.

subfiles.title: Confidential forwarding letter to Hugh R. Wilson
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department forwards confidential reports from Tokyo and several China posts.
subfiles.summary: The list includes reports on Japanese finances and conditions in Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Further copy of confidential forwarding letter
subfiles.about: A further copy lists confidential despatches sent to the American delegate at Geneva.
subfiles.summary: Its listed topics include finance problems and a visit to Peiping.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding a digest of China telegrams
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department supplies a confidential digest for possible discreet use by the League of Nations.
subfiles.summary: Gilbert may share it without revealing sources or named persons.

subfiles.title: Digest of telegrams on developments in China
subfiles.about: The digest reports opposition to Japanese borrowing and military developments in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: It summarizes criticism of bond issues and Japanese reinforcements against insurgents.

subfiles.title: Confidential letter forwarding Manchuria reports
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department forwards despatches on assassinations, cabinet rumors and Manchurian policing.
subfiles.summary: The letter lists six confidential reports from Tokyo, Mukden and Harbin.

subfiles.title: Continuation of digest on Manchurian fighting
subfiles.about: The digest reports Su Pingwen’s position and Japanese operations near Harbin.
subfiles.summary: Reports describe failed negotiations and a Japanese drive against insurgents.

subfiles.title: Confidential forwarding letter on Harbin police and bandit suppression
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department forwards reports from Harbin and Mukden.
subfiles.summary: The enclosed topics are Harbin police and bandit suppression.

subfiles.title: Confidential forwarding letter on budget estimates and Manchuria
subfiles.about: The Department lists Tokyo, Mukden and Harbin reports sent for confidential information.
subfiles.summary: One listed Tokyo despatch concerns budget estimates.

subfiles.title: Confidential forwarding letter on Mukden reports
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department sends three Mukden reports on political violence and restoration plans.
subfiles.summary: Topics include the Fushun massacre and reported plans concerning Puyi.

subfiles.title: Confidential forwarding letter on Japan and Manchukuo
subfiles.about: The Department forwards reports including one on Japan’s fiscal 1933 budget.
subfiles.summary: Other listed subjects include economic cooperation and the Fushun massacre.

subfiles.title: Confidential forwarding letter on supplementary budgets
subfiles.from: William Phillips, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department forwards Tokyo despatches on supplementary budgets and Mukden reports.
subfiles.summary: The Tokyo reports cover the 1932–33 and 1933–34 budgets.

subfiles.title: Confidential forwarding letter on financial measures
subfiles.from: William Phillips, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department forwards a report on financial measures passed by the 64th Diet.
subfiles.summary: Other reports concern Manchukuo revenues and communications.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese Army budget
subfiles.about: A cross-reference identifies an estimate of the next Japanese Army budget.
subfiles.summary: The estimate is roughly 550 million yen, twice the current budget.

subfiles.title: Summary of Japanese press articles on finance
subfiles.about: A State Department summary extracts warnings against bond-financed deficits and excessive armament spending.
subfiles.summary: It highlights proposals for retrenchment and taxes on inflation gains and investment income.

subfiles.title: Transmitting articles in regard to finance problems
subfiles.about: The embassy forwards Hijikata’s article and newspaper editorials on Japan’s budget crisis.
subfiles.summary: The despatch sees growing alarm at military demands and mounting public debt. It notes that Bank of Japan president Hijikata warns of inflation while avoiding direct opposition to military spending.

subfiles.title: Loan conversion is proposed as means of balancing budget
subfiles.about: Hijikata proposes lower bond interest and selective taxation to restrain deficit borrowing.
subfiles.summary: Hijikata warns that repeated bond issues will drive inflation and increase the yen value of foreign debt. He considers spending cuts, conversion of government loans and taxes on inflation profits and investment income, while treating Manchurian military costs as unavoidable.

subfiles.title: National Life and Defence
subfiles.about: The editorial argues that defence spending must fit national financial capacity.
subfiles.summary: It endorses Takahashi’s view that sound finances underpin armaments.

subfiles.title: The Budget of the Next Fiscal Year
subfiles.about: The editorial urges restraint in military claims and relief spending.
subfiles.summary: It warns that excessive current spending could impair later military financing.

subfiles.title: Editorial continuation on the next fiscal budget
subfiles.about: The excerpt considers reduced ministry claims and the danger of fiscal collapse.
subfiles.summary: It urges a budget matched to the state’s financial capacity.

subfiles.title: Political report section on government finance
subfiles.about: The report compares projected 1933 spending with revenue and summarizes Army, Navy and relief claims.
subfiles.summary: Projected spending reaches 2.5 billion yen, leaving a deficit above one billion yen.

subfiles.title: File note on Stimson’s conversation with the French ambassador
subfiles.about: A cross-reference identifies a conversation about Massenet’s Manchurian visit and possible French lending.
subfiles.summary: The French ambassador thought the proposed loan unlikely.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with the French ambassador
subfiles.about: The French ambassador discusses Massenet’s views on Japan and the Lytton Report.
subfiles.summary: Massenet reportedly feared a serious social crisis in Japan and worsening Japanese relations with Manchurians. The ambassador distinguished Massenet from the French government and worried that a League censure without workable proposals would hasten Japan’s decline.

subfiles.title: Confidential letter forwarding a conversation memorandum
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department sends a memorandum on a conversation with the French ambassador.
subfiles.summary: The topics are an alleged Franco-Japanese alliance and the Lytton Report.
